title: How To Handle Students Who Lie And Deny
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a classroom vignette in which a student caught misbehaving responds with aggressive denial, tempting the teacher into a your-word-against-theirs argument. He argues that lying and denying are entirely avoidable if teachers follow a disciplined three-step process rather than engaging the student's protests. The steps are knowing the truth before approaching a student, enforcing the consequence matter-of-factly without debate, and then moving on without waiting for a response. He explains that letting misbehavior play out fully before intervening removes any plausible deniability, which is what makes the enforcement step so clean. The piece closes by tying the strategy to a broader philosophy of avoidance: rather than developing better comebacks for arguments, teachers should structure their practice so the arguments never start. Linsin frames consistent, unemotional accountability as the foundation of student respect.
points: Only approach a student for a consequence once you know the truth with certainty, which requires letting misbehavior play out first.
Deliver the consequence as a flat statement of fact ('You have a warning because you broke rule number three') rather than opening a debate.
After delivering a consequence, turn and walk away immediately; waiting for a response invites arguing.
Avoiding lying-and-denying situations altogether is more effective than getting good at handling them in the moment.
Calm, truth-based, consistent accountability builds long-term student respect even in confrontational moments.
quotes: But because you’re in the good habit of letting misbehavior play out , you decide to watch a bit longer before jumping in.
But doing so would draw you into an argument. It would put you on equal footing with the student. It would turn into a your-word-against-theirs battle royal.

You should only approach a student to give a consequence when you know the truth. This underscores the importance of letting misbehavior play out, of eliminating any plausible deniability, of leaving no doubt who is responsible and what rule was broken.
With the truth on your side, there is no reason for debate. There is no reason to ask why . There is no reason to allow the student to lie to you or deny their involvement.
After delivering your consequence, turn on your heel and walk away. Nothing else needs to be said, and waiting for a response is an invitation to argue.

By calmly—even matter-of-factly—delivering your consequences with truth on your side, and then walking away, you avoid the behaviors students have used since time immemorial to sidestep accountability.

When you do what you say you will, when you handle accountability fairly and consistently, when you show your students how much you care by safeguarding their right to learn and enjoy school without interference, chaos, or drama . . .
